In this zero-count check, the $p-$value is $0.0494<0.05$ and therefore there is some evidence that the simple width-only Negative Binomial model is not reproducing the zero-count part of the response distribution. In the **training data**, the observed number of female crabs with zero satellite males is `r observed_zero_count`, while the fitted model expects only `r formatC(expected_zero_count, format = "f", digits = 2)` zeros. The difference is therefore `r formatC(observed_zero_count - expected_zero_count, format = "f", digits = 2)` additional zero counts beyond what the fitted model expects. The $p-$ value is only marginally below the $0.05$ threshold, and in comparison to the simple Classical Poisson model from [Chapter 10](https://alexrod61.github.io/regression-cookbook/book/10-classical-poisson.html), this model is a much better fit for the zero-count part of the response distribution. Recall that the $p-$value for the zero-count check in [Section 10.8.3](https://alexrod61.github.io/regression-cookbook/book/10-classical-poisson.html#sec-classical-poisson-excess-zeros) was $1.62e-20$. 

Furthermore, this zero-count check should still be interpreted as one diagnostic rather than as the only criterion for choosing a model. This situation motivates a closer look at alternatives such as zero-inflated count models.

### Residual Deviance {#sec-negative-binomial-residual-deviance}

The overdispersion and zero-count checks each focused on a specific feature of the fitted model. Note that the dispersion test (in @sec-negative-binomial-dispersion) focused on whether the observed counts vary more than what the Classical Poisson mean-variance structure allows, while the zero-count check (in @sec-negative-binomial-excess-zeros) focused on whether the model expects enough zero satellite counts.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-proud-6230200/).](img/king.png){width="400"}

Now, let us dig into **residual deviance**. This metric gives **a more global goodness-of-fit check**. Instead of focusing only on variance or zeros, it compares the likelihood of the fitted regression model with the likelihood of an idealized benchmark model that fits the observed responses as closely as possible. That benchmark is called the **saturated model**. In this chapter, we use residual deviance as another training-data diagnostic. It will help us ask whether the simple width-only Negative Binomial model is close enough to the observed training counts, relative to what would be possible under a perfect-fit benchmark.

::: {#Definition-saturated-model .definition}
:::: {.definition-header}
Definition of saturated model
::::

:::: {.definition-container}
A **saturated model** is a model that fits the observed data perfectly by using enough parameters to reproduce every observed response value exactly. The saturated model is usually not useful as a practical regression model. Instead, it serves as a theoretical benchmark. Residual deviance compares the fitted model we actually use with this perfect-fit benchmark.
::::
:::

::: {#Definition-residual-deviance .definition}
:::: {.definition-header}
Definition of residual deviance
::::

:::: {.definition-container}
The **residual deviance** of a fitted GLM measures how far the fitted regression model is from a saturated model, where the saturated model is the idealized benchmark that fits the observed responses perfectly.

The residual deviance is defined as

$$
D
=
2
\left[
\ell_{\operatorname{saturated}}
-
\ell_{\operatorname{fitted}}
\right],
$${#eq-residual-deviance}

where $\ell_{\operatorname{saturated}}$ is the log-likelihood of the saturated model, and $\ell_{\operatorname{fitted}}$ is the log-likelihood of the fitted regression model.

The factor of $2$ is included so that, under suitable regularity conditions, the residual deviance can often be compared to a Chi-squared reference distribution. In this sense, residual deviance plays a role similar to a discrepancy measure: smaller values indicate that the fitted model is closer to the saturated benchmark, while larger values indicate that the fitted model is much less likely than a model that reproduces the observed responses exactly.
::::
:::

For Negative Binomial regression, @eq-residual-deviance can be written as

$$
D
=
2
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
y_i \log\left(\frac{y_i}{\hat{\mu}_i}\right)
-
(y_i + \theta)\log\left(\frac{y_i+\theta}{\hat{\mu}_i+\theta}\right)
\right],
$${#eq-negative-binomial-residual-deviance}

where $n$ is the number of observations used to fit the model, $y_i$ is the observed count for observation $i$, $\hat{\mu}_i$ is the fitted expected count for observation $i$, and $\theta$ is the dispersion parameter. When $y_i = 0$, the term $y_i \log(y_i / \hat{\mu}_i)$ is defined to be $0$.

In practical terms, in @eq-negative-binomial-residual-deviance, the residual deviance adds up how much the observed counts differ from the fitted expected counts on the likelihood scale. It is not simply a sum of squared residuals, but it serves a similar diagnostic purpose: **it helps us assess whether the fitted model is close enough to the observed data to be considered adequate**.

If the fitted Negative Binomial model is adequate, then the gap between the fitted model and the saturated model should not be unusually large. In large samples, this gap is often assessed by comparing the residual deviance to a Chi-squared distribution with residual degrees of freedom

$$
\nu = n - (k + 1),
$$

where $n$ is the number of training observations and $k + 1$ is the number of estimated regression terms (intercept and coefficients). Under this reference approximation,

$$
D \mathrel{\sim} \chi^2_{\nu}.
$$

This gives the goodness-of-fit hypotheses

$$
\begin{gather}
H_0\text{: } \text{the fitted Negative Binomial model is adequate}, \\
\text{versus} \\
H_1\text{: } \text{the fitted Negative Binomial model is not adequate}.
\end{gather}
$$

The $p$-value is

$$
p\text{-value}
=
\Pr
\left(
\chi^2_{\nu}
\geq
D
\right).
$$

A small $p$-value means that the residual deviance is unusually large under the fitted model, which is evidence of lack of fit.

The code below extracts the residual deviance from the simple fitted model and compares it with its residual degrees of freedom:

- In `R`, `deviance(simple_poisson_width_model)` extracts the residual deviance and `df.residual(simple_poisson_width_model)` extracts the residual degrees of freedom. The upper-tail $p$-value is computed with `pchisq(..., lower.tail = FALSE)`.
- The `Python` code follows the same logic. The fitted [{statsmodels}](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html) object stores the residual deviance in `simple_poisson_width_model.deviance` and the residual degrees of freedom in `simple_poisson_width_model.df_resid`. The command `stats.chi2.sf(residual_deviance, residual_deviance_df)` computes the same upper-tail Chi-squared probability.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-residual-deviance-r
#| tbl-cap: "Residual deviance goodness-of-fit check for the simple width-only Negative Binomial regression model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Residual deviance from the fitted Poisson GLM
residual_deviance <- deviance(simple_negative_binomial_width_model)

# Residual degrees of freedom: n minus the number of estimated terms
residual_deviance_df <- df.residual(simple_negative_binomial_width_model)

# Residual deviance divided by residual degrees of freedom
residual_deviance_ratio <- residual_deviance / residual_deviance_df

# Upper-tail p-value under the Chi-squared reference distribution
residual_deviance_p_value <- pchisq(residual_deviance, df = residual_deviance_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE)

residual_deviance_summary <- tibble::tibble(`Residual deviance` = residual_deviance,
  `Residual degrees of freedom` = residual_deviance_df,
  `Residual deviance / df` = residual_deviance_ratio,
  `Goodness-of-fit p-value` = residual_deviance_p_value) |>
  mutate(`Residual deviance` = formatC(`Residual deviance`, format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Residual degrees of freedom` = formatC(`Residual degrees of freedom`, format = "f",
      digits = 0),
    `Residual deviance / df` = formatC(`Residual deviance / df`, format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Goodness-of-fit p-value` = formatC(`Goodness-of-fit p-value`, format = "e", digits = 2)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Quantity", values_to = "Value")

residual_deviance_summary |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Residual deviance from the fitted Poisson GLM
residual_deviance = simple_negative_binomial_width_model.deviance

# Residual degrees of freedom: n minus the number of estimated terms
residual_deviance_df = simple_negative_binomial_width_model.df_resid

# Residual deviance divided by residual degrees of freedom
residual_deviance_ratio = residual_deviance / residual_deviance_df

# Upper-tail p-value under the Chi-squared reference distribution
residual_deviance_p_value = stats.chi2.sf(residual_deviance, residual_deviance_df)

residual_deviance_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Quantity": ["Residual deviance", "Residual degrees of freedom",
            "Residual deviance / df", "Goodness-of-fit p-value",
        ], "Value": [f"{residual_deviance:.3f}", f"{residual_deviance_df:.0f}",
            f"{residual_deviance_ratio:.3f}", f"{residual_deviance_p_value:.2e}",
        ],
    })

classical_negative_binomial_residual_deviance_py_html = (
    scrollable_table_html(residual_deviance_summary))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-classical-negative-binomial-residual-deviance-py
#| tbl-cap: "Residual deviance goodness-of-fit check for the simple width-only Poisson regression model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  py$classical_negative_binomial_residual_deviance_py_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

For this Negative Binomial model with width as the regressor, the residual deviance is `r formatC(residual_deviance, format = "f", digits = 3)`, while the residual degrees of freedom are `r residual_deviance_df`. The ratio `r formatC(residual_deviance_ratio, format = "f", digits = 3)` is close to $1$, and the corresponding goodness-of-fit $p$-value is `r formatC(residual_deviance_p_value, format = "e", digits = 2)`. As the $p-$value is smaller than the $\alpha=0.05$, there is statistical evidence to state that this Negative Binomial regression model is correctly specified when compared to the saturated model.


Note that the residual deviance gives a single global statistic. Let's also inspect Pearson residuals against fitted expected counts. As indicated in @sec-negative-binomial-residual-deviance, Pearson residuals standardize the difference between the observed count and the fitted expected count by the Poisson standard deviation implied by the model:

$$
r_i^{(P)}
=
\frac{y_i - \hat{\mu}_i}{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_i+\frac{\hat{\mu}_i^2}{\theta}}}.
$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| label: fig-negative-binomial-pearson-residuals-r
#| fig-cap: "Pearson residuals versus fitted expected counts for the simple width-only Negative Binomial regression model. The dashed horizontal lines at -2 and 2 provide informal reference bands for large Pearson residuals."
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

pearson_residual_plot <- ggplot(simple_negative_binomial_gof_data,
  aes(x = fitted_expected_count, y = pearson_residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "solid", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#D55E00"
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, size = 2.3, colour = "#0072B2") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 20, vjust = 0.5, margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "\n Fitted expected count", y = "Pearson residual")

pearson_residual_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| label: fig-negative-binomial-pearson-residuals-py
#| fig-cap: "Pearson residuals versus fitted expected counts for the simple width-only Poisson regression model. The dashed horizontal lines at -2 and 2 provide informal reference bands for large Pearson residuals."
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: true
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

pearson_residual_figure, pearson_residual_axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))

pearson_residual_axis.axhline(0, linestyle="-", linewidth=0.8, color="grey")

pearson_residual_axis.axhline(2, linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, color="#D55E00")

pearson_residual_axis.axhline(-2, linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, color="#D55E00")

pearson_residual_axis.scatter(simple_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"],
    simple_negative_binomial_gof_data["pearson_residual"], alpha=0.65, s=35, color="#0072B2")

pearson_residual_axis.set_xlabel("\n Fitted expected count", fontsize=20)

pearson_residual_axis.set_ylabel("Pearson residual", fontsize=20, labelpad=12)

pearson_residual_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)

pearson_residual_axis.grid(True, which="major", axis="both", alpha=0.3)

pearson_residual_axis.grid(False, which="minor")

pearson_residual_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

In @fig-negative-binomial-pearson-residuals-r (or @fig-negative-binomial-pearson-residuals-py), the solid horizontal line at $0$ represents a perfect residual balance: the observed count equals the fitted expected count after standardizing by the fitted Negative Binomial standard deviation. The two dashed horizontal lines are visual reference bands at approximately $-2$ and $2$. They are not formal decision cutoffs, but they help us identify observations whose Pearson residuals are large in magnitude. Under a reasonably adequate Negative Binomial variance structure, we would expect most Pearson residuals to fall inside these bands, without a strong pattern across fitted expected counts. The residual pattern is reassuring because a majority of observations in the training are between $-2$ and $2$.


### Practical Model Adequacy {#sec-negative-binomial-practical-adequacy}

Now, we combine the diagnostic evidence. The goal is not to declare the model perfect or useless based on a single number. Instead, we ask whether the simple width-only Negative Binomial model is adequate enough for the next stage of the workflow.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-teaching-to-learn-wiki-3976301/).](img/board.png){width="500"}

| **Diagnostic** | **What we checked** | **What the training data suggest** | **Practical implication** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Observed versus fitted counts | Whether fitted expected counts track observed counts across the training data. | The model captures a broad increase in expected counts with width, and individual counts show large variability around the fitted expectations (see @fig-classical-poisson-observed-fitted-r or @fig-classical-poisson-observed-fitted-py). | Width is useful and the simple model is a good fit for the satellite counts. |
| Pearson overdispersion test | Whether the conditional variance is compatible with the Negative Binomial mean-variance structure. | The Pearson dispersion estimate is close to $1$, and the overdispersion $p$-value is large. | The Negative Binomial model gives **larger standard errors** for regression coefficients than the Classical Poisson model, meaning that the Negative Binomial model is less prone to **false positive** errors. |
| Zero-count check | Whether the fitted model expects a similar number of zeros as observed. | If the observed zero count is larger than the fitted expected zero count, the model is not reproducing the zero-count part of the distribution. | Excess zeros may motivate a **zero-inflated model** in a later chapter. |
| Residual deviance | Whether the fitted model is close enough to a saturated benchmark. | The residual deviance is close to the degrees of freedom, with a goodness-of-fit $p$-value>0.05. | There is statistical evidence of good fit in the width-only Negative Binomial model. |
| Pearson residual plot | Whether residuals show unusually large discrepancies relative to the fitted Poisson variance. | Large residuals and broad residual spread support the overdispersion conclusion (see @fig-classical-poisson-pearson-residuals-r or @fig-classical-poisson-pearson-residuals-py). | The simple model is adequate as an inferential model for the relationship between female crab width and satellite counts. |

: Summary of goodness-of-fit findings for the simple width-only Negative Binomial regression model fit on the training data. {#tbl-simple-classical-poisson-gof-summary .striped .hover}

As the overall diagnostic picture was not favourable for the [Classical Poisson model](https://alexrod61.github.io/regression-cookbook/book/10-classical-poisson.html#sec-classical-poisson-practical-adequacy), we decided to fit the Negative Binomial model. The overall diagnostic picture is favourable for this simple Negative Binomial model. The model not only captures the relationship between **female crab width** and **satellite male counts** in the population but also adequately explains the large variability in the observed satellite counts in the train set. The zero-count check does not indicate substantial underestimation in the number of zero counts; however, there is some statistical evidence that this model is not reproducing the zero-count portion of the response distribution. There is statistical evidence to state that the simple Negative Binomial is correctly specified in comparison to the saturated model.

## Extending the Model with Additional Regressors {#sec-negative-binomial-additional-regressors}

In @tbl-simple-negative-binomial-gof-summary, the goodness-of-fit checks for the simple width-only model showed that it is a good start. The model captured a useful width-based mean pattern, and adequately reproduced the variability in the response variable. In the data science workflow, this is a natural point to return to the **data modelling** and **estimation** stages rather than moving directly to final conclusions.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-help-assistance-3974184/).](img/fixing.png){width="550"}

We now extend the Negative Binomial regression model by adding the remaining regressors available in the horseshoe crab dataset. Hence, this means retaking the same modelling cycle: 

1. Define the model notation carefully.
2. Encode the categorical regressors using dummy variables.
3. Estimate the extended model on the training data.
4. Revisit goodness of fit on the training data.
5. Interpret the fitted mean structure, and prepare predictions for held-out testing observations.

We still fit and diagnose the model using the **training data**. Then, the testing data remain reserved for the later **results section**, where we will evaluate final predictive performance and produce final inferential outputs according to the chapter workflow.

### Adding Phenotypic Regressors {#sec-classical-poisson-phenotypic-regressors}

Recall the notation introduced in @tbl-negative-binomial-variables. The response is $Y_i$, the observed number of satellite males for the $i$th female crab. The continuous regressors are:

- $x_{i,1}$: female crab carapace width in centimetres;
- $x_{i,2}$: female crab weight in kilograms.

The remaining regressors are categorical. As in the data modelling example from @sec-intro-negative-binomial, we represent categorical variables by creating binary dummy variables (see @tbl-negative-binomial-dummy-variables). If a categorical variable has $u$ levels, we use $u - 1$ dummy variables and leave one level as the baseline or reference category. The baseline category is represented by all zeros for that categorical variable.

Before defining the dummy variables, we first verify the order of the categorical levels. This is necessary because the baseline category is the level represented by all dummy variables equal to zero. For this model, `Light` is the baseline category for `color` and `Both good` is the baseline category for `spine` since these two categories appear on the left-hand side of the coding output.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-levels-color-spine-r
#| lst-cap: "Code to check colour and spine levels."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

levels(training_data$color)
levels(training_data$spine)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-levels-color-spine-py
#| lst-cap: "Code to relevel colour and spine levels."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

color_order = ["Light", "Medium light", "Medium dark", "Dark",
]

spine_order = ["Both good", "One worn or broken", "Both worn or broken",
]

training_data["color"] = pd.Categorical(training_data["color"], categories=color_order)

training_data["spine"] = pd.Categorical(training_data["spine"], categories=spine_order)

training_data["color"].cat.categories

training_data["spine"].cat.categories
```

:::

For `color`, we use `Light` as the baseline category. Since `color` has four levels, we need three dummy variables:

$$
x_{i,3}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the } i\text{th female crab has colour Medium light}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise};
\end{cases}
$$

$$
x_{i,4}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the } i\text{th female crab has colour Medium dark}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise};
\end{cases}
$$

and

$$
x_{i,5}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the } i\text{th female crab has colour Dark}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus, a female crab in the `Light` colour category has

$$
x_{i,3}=x_{i,4}=x_{i,5}=0.
$$

For `spine`, we use `Both good` as the baseline category. Since `spine` has three levels, we need two dummy variables:

$$
x_{i,6}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the } i\text{th female crab has one worn or broken spine}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise};
\end{cases}
$$

and

$$
x_{i,7}
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if the } i\text{th female crab has both spines worn or broken}, \\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus, a female crab in the `Both good` spine category has

$$
x_{i,6}=x_{i,7}=0.
$$

The full dummy-variable arrangement is summarized in @tbl-negative-binomial-dummy-variable-arrangement.

| Original variable | Baseline category | Dummy variable | Dummy equals $1$ when... | Dummy equals $0$ when... |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `color` | `Light` | $x_{i,3}$ | `color` is `Medium light` | otherwise |
| `color` | `Light` | $x_{i,4}$ | `color` is `Medium dark` | otherwise |
| `color` | `Light` | $x_{i,5}$ | `color` is `Dark` | otherwise |
| `spine` | `Both good` | $x_{i,6}$ | `spine` is `One worn or broken` | otherwise |
| `spine` | `Both good` | $x_{i,7}$ | `spine` is `Both worn or broken` | otherwise |

: Dummy-variable arrangement for the categorical regressors in the extended horseshoe crab Negative Binomial regression model. {#tbl-negative-binomial-dummy-variable-arrangement .striped .hover}

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on reference categories and dummy variables!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
The reference category is not omitted because it is unimportant. It is omitted from the dummy-variable list because its information is carried by the intercept and by the fact that all dummy variables for that categorical regressor equal zero.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-upset-6230193/).](img/surprise-2.png){width="300"}

For colour, `Light` is the reference category. For spine condition, `Both good` is the reference category. Therefore, categorical coefficients in the extended model are interpreted relative to these baseline categories, holding the other regressors fixed.
::::
:::

Using this notation, the extended Negative Binomial regression model is

$$
Y_i \mid x_{i,1}, x_{i,2}, \ldots, x_{i,7}
\sim
\operatorname{Negative Binomial}(\mu_i, \theta),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
\log(\mu_i)
=
&\ \beta_0
+
\beta_1 x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2 x_{i,2}
+
\beta_3 x_{i,3}
+
\beta_4 x_{i,4} \\
&+
\beta_5 x_{i,5}
+
\beta_6 x_{i,6}
+
\beta_7 x_{i,7}.
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-classical-poisson-extended-model}

Equivalently,

$$
\mu_i
=
\exp
\left(
\beta_0
+
\beta_1 x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2 x_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_7 x_{i,7}
\right).
$${#eq-negative-binomial-extended-mean}

This extended model uses the same Negative Binomial random component and log link as before. What changes is the **systematic component**: instead of using width alone, we now use width, weight, and dummy variables for colour and spine condition.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on adding regressors after a failed goodness-of-fit check!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
Adding regressors can improve a model when the original systematic component was too simple. For example, if weight, colour, or spine condition explain differences in satellite counts that width alone did not capture, then the extended model may fit the training data better.

However, adding regressors does not automatically fix overdispersion or excess zeros. Overdispersion and zero inflation are distributional problems, not only mean-structure problems. Therefore, after fitting the extended Negative Binomial model, we must repeat the goodness-of-fit checks rather than assuming that the additional regressors solved the diagnostic issues.
::::
:::

Now, we fit the extended model on the training data:

- In `R`, the formula `satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine` tells `glm()` to create the needed dummy variables for the categorical regressors automatically, using the first factor level as the reference category. 
- In `Python`, via @lst-levels-color-spine-py, we explicitly set the categorical order and reference categories so that the fitted model matches the same dummy-variable setup. Then, we fit the corresponding extended model.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-extended-model-fit-r
#| tbl-cap: "Maximum likelihood estimates from the extended Negative Binomial regression model fitted on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_negative_binomial_model <- glm.nb(satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine, 
                                           data = training_data)

extended_negative_binomial_summary <- tidy(extended_negative_binomial_model) |>
  dplyr::mutate(exponentiated_estimate = exp(estimate),
    percent_change = 100 * (exponentiated_estimate - 1),
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
    dplyr::select(term, estimate, std.error, exponentiated_estimate, percent_change)

extended_negative_binomial_summary |>
  rename(`Term` = term, `Estimate` = estimate, `Standard error` = std.error,
    `Exponentiated estimate` = exponentiated_estimate, `Percent change` = percent_change) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_negative_binomial_alpha = smf.negativebinomial(
    "satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine", data=training_data
).fit(disp=0).params["alpha"]

extended_negative_binomial_model = smf.glm(
    "satellites ~ width_cm + weight_kg + color + spine",
    data=training_data,
    family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(alpha=extended_negative_binomial_alpha),
).fit()

extended_negative_binomial_summary = (
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "Term": extended_negative_binomial_model.params.index,
            "Estimate": extended_negative_binomial_model.params.values,
            "Standard error": extended_negative_binomial_model.bse.values,
        }
    )
    .assign(
        **{
            "Exponentiated estimate": lambda df: np.exp(df["Estimate"]),
            "Percent change": lambda df: 100 * (np.exp(df["Estimate"]) - 1),
        }
    )
    .round(2)
)

negative_binomial_extended_model_fit_py_html = scrollable_table_html(extended_negative_binomial_summary)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-negative_binomial-extended-model-fit-py
#| tbl-cap: "Maximum likelihood estimates from the extended Poisson regression model fitted on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  py$negative_binomial_extended_model_fit_py_html,
  "\n",
  sep = "")
```

:::

@tbl-negative-binomial-extended-model-fit-r reports estimates, model-based standard errors, exponentiated estimates, and percent changes. We intentionally do **not** conduct Wald tests here. Hypothesis testing and final coefficient-level inferential decisions are saved for the later **results section**, after the model-building workflow has been completed.

### Extended Goodness-of-Fit Checks {#sec-negative-binomial-extended-gof}

Now, before interpreting the coefficients, we repeat the goodness-of-fit checks for the extended model. Since the simple width-only model showed overdispersion, excess zeros, and a large residual deviance, we now ask whether adding `weight_kg`, `color`, and `spine` improved those same diagnostics. We will use the same diagnostic tools developed for the simple model, but we will organize them more efficiently here. The goal is not to rederive the mathematics. Instead, we reuse the same ideas to assess whether the extended Negative Binomial model is more adequate on the training data.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-teacher-acrobatics-3974168/).](img/sequence.png){width="700"}

#### Regressor Correlation Structure

Before computing any diagnostic quantities, it is worth looking at how the regressors in the extended model relate to one another. Recall from the exploratory data analysis in @sec-negative-binomial-eda-continuous that width and weight are both body-size measurements, so they may carry partly overlapping information. The heatmap below makes that overlap explicit by reporting the pairwise correlations among the **columns of the model matrix**, i.e., the two continuous regressors together with the five dummy variables from @tbl-negative-binomial-dummy-variable-arrangement. These are the quantities the model actually estimates coefficients for, so this is the correlation structure that is relevant when we interpret those coefficients.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| label: fig-negative-binomial-extended-regressor-correlation-r
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise correlations among the regressors in the extended Negative Binomial regression model, computed on the training data."
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

extended_regressor_matrix <- model.matrix(extended_negative_binomial_model)[, -1, drop = FALSE]

colnames(extended_regressor_matrix) <- gsub("^(color|spine)", "\\1 ",
  colnames(extended_regressor_matrix))

extended_regressor_correlation <- cor(extended_regressor_matrix)

extended_regressor_order <- colnames(extended_regressor_correlation)

extended_regressor_correlation_long <- as.data.frame(extended_regressor_correlation,
  check.names = FALSE) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("regressor_row") |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(cols = -regressor_row, names_to = "regressor_column",
    values_to = "correlation") |>
  mutate(regressor_row = factor(regressor_row, levels = extended_regressor_order),
    regressor_column = factor(regressor_column, levels = rev(extended_regressor_order)))

extended_regressor_correlation_plot <- ggplot(extended_regressor_correlation_long,
  aes(x = regressor_row, y = regressor_column, fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = formatC(correlation, format = "f", digits = 2)), size = 5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#0072B2", mid = "white", high = "#D55E00",
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "Correlation") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 13, angle = 35, hjust = 1),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 13),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16), legend.text = element_text(size = 13),
    panel.grid = element_blank()) +
  coord_fixed()

extended_regressor_correlation_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| label: fig-negative-binomial-extended-regressor-correlation-py
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise correlations among the regressors in the extended Negative Binomial regression model, computed on the training data."
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

# Importing function
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

extended_regressor_matrix = pd.DataFrame(
    extended_negative_binomial_model.model.exog,
    columns=extended_negative_binomial_model.model.exog_names).drop(columns="Intercept")

extended_regressor_matrix.columns = (extended_regressor_matrix.columns
    .str.replace(r"\[T\.(.+)\]", r" \1", regex=True))

extended_regressor_order = ["width_cm", "weight_kg", "color Medium light",
    "color Medium dark", "color Dark", "spine One worn or broken",
    "spine Both worn or broken"]

extended_regressor_correlation = (extended_regressor_matrix[extended_regressor_order].corr())

extended_correlation_colormap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list(
    "extended_correlation_colormap", ["#0072B2", "#FFFFFF", "#D55E00"])

extended_correlation_figure, extended_correlation_axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))

extended_correlation_image = extended_correlation_axis.imshow(
    extended_regressor_correlation.values, cmap=extended_correlation_colormap,
    vmin=-1, vmax=1)

extended_correlation_axis.set_xticks(range(len(extended_regressor_correlation.columns)))

extended_correlation_axis.set_xticklabels(extended_regressor_correlation.columns,
    rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=13)

extended_correlation_axis.set_yticks(range(len(extended_regressor_correlation.index)))

extended_correlation_axis.set_yticklabels(extended_regressor_correlation.index, fontsize=13)

for row_index in range(len(extended_regressor_correlation.index)):
    for column_index in range(len(extended_regressor_correlation.columns)):
        extended_correlation_axis.text(column_index, row_index,
            f"{extended_regressor_correlation.iloc[row_index, column_index]:.2f}",
            ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13)

extended_correlation_colorbar = extended_correlation_figure.colorbar(
    extended_correlation_image, ax=extended_correlation_axis, shrink=0.85)

extended_correlation_colorbar.set_label("Correlation", fontsize=16)

extended_correlation_colorbar.ax.tick_params(labelsize=13)

extended_correlation_axis.grid(False)

extended_correlation_figure.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

Two points are worth making about @fig-negative-binomial-extended-regressor-correlation-r before we move on.

First, the cell relating `width_cm` and `weight_kg` is the one that carries genuine information about the data. A large positive correlation there would confirm the EDA concern that the two body-size regressors overlap, which in turn means their individual coefficients in the extended model should be interpreted with care. Each coefficient is a *conditional* association, holding the other regressor fixed, and that conditioning becomes harder to interpret when the two regressors move together in the training data.

Second, the blocks involving the `color` and `spine` dummy variables will show negative correlations **by construction**, not because of anything in the horseshoe crab data. Two dummy variables built from the same categorical regressor cannot both equal $1$ for the same female crab, so they are mechanically negatively related. This is a good reminder that a correlation heatmap describes the design matrix, not the scientific structure of the problem. When we want a formal collinearity diagnostic that handles categorical regressors properly, a variance inflation factor, such as the generalized variance inflation factor reported by `car::vif()`, is the more appropriate tool.

#### Creating Extended-Model Diagnostic Quantities

The first step is to create the **fitted expected counts**, **Pearson residuals**, and **fitted zero probabilities** for the extended model. These are the same diagnostic quantities used for the simple model in @sec-classical-poisson-gof, but now they come from the model with all available regressors.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_negative_binomial_gof_data <- training_data |>
  mutate(fitted_expected_count = fitted(extended_negative_binomial_model),
    pearson_residual = (satellites - fitted_expected_count) / sqrt(fitted_expected_count + fitted_expected_count^2 / extended_negative_binomial_model$theta),
    fitted_zero_probability = (extended_negative_binomial_model$theta /
      (extended_negative_binomial_model$theta + fitted_expected_count))^extended_negative_binomial_model$theta)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
extended_negative_binomial_alpha = extended_negative_binomial_model.family.alpha
extended_negative_binomial_gof_data = training_data.copy()
extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"] = (extended_negative_binomial_model.fittedvalues)
extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["pearson_residual"] = ((extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["satellites"]
        - extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"])
    / np.sqrt(extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"]
        + extended_negative_binomial_alpha * extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"] ** 2))
extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_zero_probability"] = (
    1 + extended_negative_binomial_alpha * extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_expected_count"]) ** (
    -1 / extended_negative_binomial_alpha)
```

:::

These quantities let us reuse the same goodness-of-fit logic from the simple model from @sec-negative-binomial-observed-fitted. The fitted expected counts $\hat{\mu}_i$ summarize the fitted mean structure, the Pearson residuals (see @eq-pearson-residual) compare observed and fitted counts relative to the fitted Negative Binomial standard deviation, and the fitted zero probabilities $\exp(-\hat{\mu}_i)$ tell us how often the extended model expects zero satellite counts.

#### Extended Observed versus Fitted Counts

Before revisiting overdispersion, zero counts, and residual deviance, we first compare the **observed satellite counts** with the **fitted expected counts** from the extended model. This mirrors the observed-versus-fitted check from @sec--observed-fitted, but now the fitted expected counts come from the model that includes width, weight, colour, and spine condition. This check is still based on the **training data**. The goal is not to measure held-out prediction accuracy yet. Instead, we are asking whether the extended model’s fitted expected counts are better aligned with the observed count distribution than the simple width-only model.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-star-star-hour-reward-3974182/).](img/stars.png){width="550"}

We start by grouping observations into quartiles based on their fitted expected counts. Within each group, we compare the mean observed count with the mean fitted expected count and also compare the observed zero proportion with the average fitted probability of zero satellite counts.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl--extended-fitted-count-calibration-r
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted satellite counts across fitted expected count quartiles for the extended Negative Binomial regression model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_fitted_count_calibration <- extended_negative_binomial_gof_data |>
  mutate(fitted_count_quartile = ntile(fitted_expected_count, 4),
    fitted_count_quartile = factor(fitted_count_quartile, levels = 1:4,
      labels = c("Q1: smallest fitted counts", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4: largest fitted counts"))) |>
  group_by(fitted_count_quartile) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_observed_count = mean(satellites),
    mean_fitted_expected_count = mean(fitted_expected_count),
    observed_zero_proportion = mean(satellites == 0),
    mean_fitted_zero_probability = mean(fitted_zero_probability),.groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

extended_fitted_count_calibration |>
  rename(`Fitted-count quartile` = fitted_count_quartile, `Number of female crabs` = n,
    `Mean observed count` = mean_observed_count,
    `Mean fitted expected count` = mean_fitted_expected_count,
    `Observed zero proportion` = observed_zero_proportion,
    `Average fitted probability of zero satellites` = mean_fitted_zero_probability) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_fitted_count_calibration_data = extended_negative_binomial_gof_data.copy()

extended_fitted_count_calibration_data = (extended_fitted_count_calibration_data
    .sort_values("fitted_expected_count", kind="mergesort").reset_index(drop=True))

number_of_rows = len(extended_fitted_count_calibration_data)
number_of_groups = 4

base_group_size = number_of_rows // number_of_groups
remainder = number_of_rows % number_of_groups

group_sizes = [base_group_size + 1 if group_index < remainder else base_group_size
    for group_index in range(number_of_groups)]

fitted_count_quartile_labels = ["Q1: smallest fitted counts", "Q2", "Q3",
    "Q4: largest fitted counts",
]

extended_fitted_count_calibration_data["fitted_count_quartile"] = np.repeat(
    fitted_count_quartile_labels, group_sizes)

extended_fitted_count_calibration_data["fitted_count_quartile"] = (
    pd.Categorical(extended_fitted_count_calibration_data["fitted_count_quartile"],
        categories=fitted_count_quartile_labels, ordered=True))

extended_fitted_count_calibration = (extended_fitted_count_calibration_data
    .groupby("fitted_count_quartile", observed=False)
    .agg(n=("satellites", "size"), mean_observed_count=("satellites", "mean"),
        mean_fitted_expected_count=("fitted_expected_count", "mean"),
        observed_zero_proportion=("satellites", lambda x: (x == 0).mean()),
        mean_fitted_zero_probability=("fitted_zero_probability", "mean"),
    ).reset_index().round(3))

extended_fitted_count_calibration_display = (extended_fitted_count_calibration
    .rename(columns={"fitted_count_quartile": "Fitted-count quartile",
            "n": "Number of female crabs", "mean_observed_count": "Mean observed count",
            "mean_fitted_expected_count": "Mean fitted expected count",
            "observed_zero_proportion": "Observed zero proportion",
            "mean_fitted_zero_probability": ("Average fitted probability of zero satellites"
            ),
        }))

classical_negative_binomial_extended_fitted_count_calibration_py_html = (
    scrollable_table_html(extended_fitted_count_calibration_display))
```

:::

In @fig-negative-binomial-extended-observed-fitted-r, the dashed line marks where the observed satellite count would equal the fitted expected count. Points above the line correspond to female crabs whose observed counts are larger than the extended model expects, while points below the line correspond to female crabs whose observed counts are smaller than expected. The plot shows that the extended model still has important calibration problems. Many observations with fitted expected counts between roughly $1.5$ and $4$ have observed counts of $0$, so they sit below the dashed line. This agrees with the grouped calibration in @tbl-negative-binomial-extended-fitted-count-calibration-r; the extended model underestimates the proportions of zero counts in the lower half of the fitted values and overestimates zero counts in the upper half of fitted values. At the same time, several observations in the same fitted-count range have observed counts around $6$, $8$, $10$, or even $12$, placing them far above the dashed line.

The horizontal bands are expected because the observed response is a count. The fitted expected count on the $x$-axis is allowed to be fractional, but the observed satellite count on the $y$-axis can only take values such as $0, 1, 2, 3$, and so on. What is concerning is not the banding itself, but the wide vertical spread among observations with similar fitted expected counts.

#### Extended Overdispersion Check


#### Extended Zero-Count Check

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-download-data-transfer-3947910/).](img/pulling.png){width="600"}

Next, we check whether the extended model expects **enough zero counts** as in @sec-negative-binomial-excess-zeros. Recall that this diagnostic focuses on the number of observed zero counts,

$$
z_{\operatorname{obs}}
=
\sum_{i=1}^n
\mathbb{1}(y_i = 0),
$$

where $\mathbb{1}(y_i = 0)$ is an indicator that equals $1$ when the $i$th observed satellite count is zero and equals $0$ otherwise. Furthermore, in this goodness-of-fit check for a one-sided test, the hypotheses are:

$$
\begin{gather}
H_0\text{: } \text{the fitted Negative Binomial model adequately describes} \\
\text{the frequency of zero counts}, \\
\text{versus} \\
H_1\text{: } \text{there are more zero counts than the} \\
\text{fitted Negative Binomial model expects},
\end{gather}
$$

with an approximate $z$-statistic as in @eq-z-statistic-zero-counts.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-extended-zero-count-r
#| tbl-cap: "Excess zero-count diagnostic for the extended Negative Binomial regression model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_observed_zero_count <- sum(extended_negative_binomial_gof_data$satellites == 0)

extended_expected_zero_count <- sum(extended_negative_binomial_gof_data$fitted_zero_probability)

extended_zero_count_variance <- sum(extended_negative_binomial_gof_data$fitted_zero_probability *
    (1 - extended_negative_binomial_gof_data$fitted_zero_probability))

extended_zero_count_z <- (extended_observed_zero_count - extended_expected_zero_count
) / sqrt(extended_zero_count_variance)

extended_zero_count_p_value <- pnorm(extended_zero_count_z, lower.tail = FALSE)

extended_zero_count_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  `Observed zero count` = extended_observed_zero_count,
  `Fitted expected zero count` = extended_expected_zero_count,
  `Observed minus fitted zeros` = (
    extended_observed_zero_count - extended_expected_zero_count),
  `Zero-count z-statistic` = extended_zero_count_z,
  `Zero-count p-value` = extended_zero_count_p_value) |>
  mutate(`Observed zero count` = formatC(`Observed zero count`, format = "f", digits = 0),
    `Fitted expected zero count` = formatC(`Fitted expected zero count`, format = "f",
      digits = 2),
    `Observed minus fitted zeros` = formatC(`Observed minus fitted zeros`, format = "f",
      digits = 2),
    `Zero-count z-statistic` = formatC(`Zero-count z-statistic`, format = "f", digits = 2),
    `Zero-count p-value` = formatC(`Zero-count p-value`, format = "e", digits = 2)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Quantity", values_to = "Value")

extended_zero_count_summary |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

extended_observed_zero_count = (extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["satellites"] == 0).sum()

extended_expected_zero_count = (extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_zero_probability"].sum())

extended_zero_count_variance = (extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_zero_probability"]
    * (1 - extended_negative_binomial_gof_data["fitted_zero_probability"])).sum()

extended_zero_count_z = (extended_observed_zero_count - extended_expected_zero_count
) / np.sqrt(extended_zero_count_variance)

extended_zero_count_p_value = stats.norm.sf(extended_zero_count_z)

extended_zero_count_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Quantity": ["Observed zero count", "Fitted expected zero count",
            "Observed minus fitted zeros", "Zero-count z-statistic", "Zero-count p-value",
        ], "Value": [f"{extended_observed_zero_count:.0f}",
            f"{extended_expected_zero_count:.2f}",
            f"{extended_observed_zero_count - extended_expected_zero_count:.2f}",
            f"{extended_zero_count_z:.2f}", f"{extended_zero_count_p_value:.2e}",
        ],
    })

negative_binomial_extended_zero_count_py_html = (
    scrollable_table_html(extended_zero_count_summary))
```

```{r}
#| message: false

cat(
  "\n",
  py$negative_binomial_extended_zero_count_py_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""

```

:::


The extended model shows a significant zero-count mismatch. In the **training data**, we observe `r extended_observed_zero_count` female crabs with zero satellite males, but the fitted extended Negative Binomial model expects only `r formatC(extended_expected_zero_count, format = "f", digits = 2)` zeros. This leaves `r formatC(extended_observed_zero_count - extended_expected_zero_count, format = "f", digits = 2)` additional observed zeros beyond what the fitted model expects. Moreover, the approximate zero-count $z$-statistic is `r formatC(extended_zero_count_z, format = "f", digits = 2)`, with a one-sided $p$-value of `r formatC(extended_zero_count_p_value, format = "e", digits = 2)`. This provides strong evidence that the extended model is understating the zero-count part of the response distribution.

Compared with the simple width-only model, adding weight, colour, and spine condition gives the fitted mean structure more flexibility; however, the extended Negative Binomial model still expects **far fewer zero satellite counts than we actually observe**. This suggests that the Negative Binomial distribution struggles to represent how often zero satellite counts occur in the train set.

#### Model Selection

We can use analysis of deviance for model selection when two models. The simple width-only Negative Binomial model (i.e. `simple_negative_binomial_model` from [Section 11.7](http://localhost:54321/book/11-negative-binomial.html#sec-negative-binomial-simple-model)) is nested within the extended Negative Binomial model (i.e. `extended_negative_binomial_model`). We will test our two Negative Binomial models using `deviance` function in `R` and .... in `Python`. The model section involves a hypothesis testing. The hypotheses are
$$
begin{gather*}
H_0: \textbf{Simple Model} \text{ fits the data better than } \textbf{Extended Model} \\
H_a: \textbf{Extended} \text{ fits the data better than } \textbf{Simple Model}.
\end{gather*}
$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-nested-deviance-r
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis of deviance comparing the simple width-only and extended Negative Binomial regression models on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Dispersion parameter from the extended model, held common across both fits
extended_negative_binomial_theta <- extended_negative_binomial_model$theta

# Refitting the reduced width-only model at the common dispersion parameter
nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model <- glm(formula = satellites ~ width_cm,
  family = negative.binomial(theta = extended_negative_binomial_theta),
  data = training_data)

# Residual deviances from the reduced and extended models
nested_reduced_deviance <- deviance(nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model)

nested_extended_deviance <- deviance(extended_negative_binomial_model)

# Deviance difference: the likelihood-ratio test statistic
nested_deviance_statistic <- nested_reduced_deviance - nested_extended_deviance

# Degrees of freedom: the number of additional estimated regression coefficients
nested_deviance_df <- df.residual(nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model) -
  df.residual(extended_negative_binomial_model)

# Upper-tail p-value under the Chi-squared reference distribution
nested_deviance_p_value <- pchisq(nested_deviance_statistic, df = nested_deviance_df,
  lower.tail = FALSE)

nested_deviance_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  `Reduced model residual deviance` = nested_reduced_deviance,
  `Extended model residual deviance` = nested_extended_deviance,
  `Deviance difference` = nested_deviance_statistic,
  `Degrees of freedom` = nested_deviance_df,
  `p-value` = nested_deviance_p_value) |>
  mutate(`Reduced model residual deviance` = formatC(`Reduced model residual deviance`,
      format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Extended model residual deviance` = formatC(`Extended model residual deviance`,
      format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Deviance difference` = formatC(`Deviance difference`, format = "f", digits = 3),
    `Degrees of freedom` = formatC(`Degrees of freedom`, format = "f", digits = 0),
    `p-value` = formatC(`p-value`, format = "e", digits = 2)) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Quantity", values_to = "Value")

nested_deviance_summary |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Dispersion parameter from the extended model, held common across both fits
extended_negative_binomial_alpha = extended_negative_binomial_model.family.alpha

# Refitting the reduced width-only model at the common dispersion parameter
nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model = smf.glm(formula="satellites ~ width_cm",
    data=training_data, family=sm.families.NegativeBinomial(
        alpha=extended_negative_binomial_alpha)).fit(scale=1.0)

# Residual deviances from the reduced and extended models
nested_reduced_deviance = nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model.deviance

nested_extended_deviance = extended_negative_binomial_model.deviance

# Deviance difference: the likelihood-ratio test statistic
nested_deviance_statistic = nested_reduced_deviance - nested_extended_deviance

# Degrees of freedom: the number of additional estimated regression coefficients
nested_deviance_df = (nested_reduced_negative_binomial_model.df_resid
    - extended_negative_binomial_model.df_resid)

# Upper-tail p-value under the Chi-squared reference distribution
nested_deviance_p_value = stats.chi2.sf(nested_deviance_statistic, nested_deviance_df)

nested_deviance_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Quantity": ["Reduced model residual deviance", "Extended model residual deviance",
            "Deviance difference", "Degrees of freedom", "p-value",
        ], "Value": [f"{nested_reduced_deviance:.3f}", f"{nested_extended_deviance:.3f}",
            f"{nested_deviance_statistic:.3f}", f"{nested_deviance_df:.0f}",
            f"{nested_deviance_p_value:.2e}",
        ],
    })

negative_binomial_nested_deviance_py_html = (
    scrollable_table_html(nested_deviance_summary))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-nested-deviance-py
#| tbl-cap: "Analysis of deviance comparing the simple width-only and extended Negative Binomial regression models on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  py$negative_binomial_nested_deviance_py_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

The test statistic for the analysis of deviance is the difference between the residual deviance of `simple_negative_binomial_model` and the residual deviance `extended_negative_binomial_model`. The test statistic ($\Delta_D$) is asymptotically (i.e.,$n\rightarrow\infty$) Chi-squared distributed with $6$ degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis $H_0$. The value of $\Delta_D$ is `r round(nested_deviance_statistic,3)` with a $p-$value of `r round(nested_deviance_p_value,2)`. As the $p-$value is larger than $\alpha=0.05$, we fail to reject the null hypothesis and there is statistical evidence to state that the extended Negative Binomial model is misspecified for the crabs data in comparison to the width-only Negative Binomial Model.

Let's compare the AIC scores of `simple_negative_binomial_model` and `extended_negative_binomial_model`.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

````{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-aic-comparison-r
#| tbl-cap: "Akaike Information Criterion for the simple width-only and extended Negative Binomial regression models fitted on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# AIC for each model, counting the estimated dispersion parameter
simple_negative_binomial_aic <- AIC(simple_negative_binomial_width_model)

extended_negative_binomial_aic <- AIC(extended_negative_binomial_model)

# Estimated parameters: regression coefficients plus the dispersion parameter
simple_negative_binomial_parameters <- length(coef(simple_negative_binomial_width_model)) + 1

extended_negative_binomial_parameters <- length(coef(extended_negative_binomial_model)) + 1

# Difference from the best-scoring model
negative_binomial_minimum_aic <- min(c(simple_negative_binomial_aic,
  extended_negative_binomial_aic))

negative_binomial_aic_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  `Model` = c("Simple (width only)", "Extended (all regressors)"),
  `Estimated parameters` = c(simple_negative_binomial_parameters,
    extended_negative_binomial_parameters),
  `AIC` = c(simple_negative_binomial_aic, extended_negative_binomial_aic))|>
  mutate(`Estimated parameters` = formatC(`Estimated parameters`, format = "f", digits = 0),
    `AIC` = formatC(`AIC`, format = "f", digits = 3))

negative_binomial_aic_summary |>
  kable(align = c("l", "c", "c", "c"))
````

## **`Python`**

````{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# Estimated parameters: regression coefficients plus the dispersion parameter
simple_negative_binomial_parameters = len(simple_negative_binomial_width_model.params) + 1

extended_negative_binomial_parameters = len(extended_negative_binomial_model.params) + 1

# AIC computed from the maximized log-likelihood so that the dispersion
# parameter is counted, matching the convention used by glm.nb() in R
simple_negative_binomial_aic = (-2 * simple_negative_binomial_width_model.llf
    + 2 * simple_negative_binomial_parameters)

extended_negative_binomial_aic = (-2 * extended_negative_binomial_model.llf
    + 2 * extended_negative_binomial_parameters)

# Difference from the best-scoring model
negative_binomial_minimum_aic = min(simple_negative_binomial_aic,
    extended_negative_binomial_aic)

negative_binomial_aic_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {"Model": ["Simple (width only)", "Extended (all regressors)"],
        "Estimated parameters": [f"{simple_negative_binomial_parameters:.0f}",
            f"{extended_negative_binomial_parameters:.0f}",
        ], "AIC": [f"{simple_negative_binomial_aic:.3f}",
            f"{extended_negative_binomial_aic:.3f}",
        ], "AIC difference": [
            f"{simple_negative_binomial_aic - negative_binomial_minimum_aic:.3f}",
            f"{extended_negative_binomial_aic - negative_binomial_minimum_aic:.3f}",
        ],
    })

negative_binomial_aic_comparison_py_html = (
    scrollable_table_html(negative_binomial_aic_summary))
````

````{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-negative-binomial-aic-comparison-py
#| tbl-cap: "Akaike Information Criterion for the simple width-only and extended Negative Binomial regression models fitted on the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  py$negative_binomial_aic_comparison_py_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
````

:::

The simple width-only model has an AIC of `r formatC(simple_negative_binomial_aic, format = "f", digits = 3)` against `r formatC(extended_negative_binomial_aic, format = "f", digits = 3)` for the extended model, which is a difference of `r formatC(abs(simple_negative_binomial_aic - extended_negative_binomial_aic), format = "f", digits = 2)`. The deviance test asks whether the additional regressors provide statistically significant increase in likelihood at a fixed $\alpha$ level, whereas AIC asks whether that improvement is large enough to justify the additional parameters under a specific complexity penalty. 

#### Extended Goodness-of-Fit Summary

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-social-network-3704066/).](img/privacy.png){width="500"}

The extended-model diagnostics are summarized in @tbl-negative-binomial-extended-gof-summary. This table brings together the main evidence from the observed-versus-fitted comparison, the Pearson overdispersion check, the zero-count check, and the residual deviance check.

| Diagnostic | Main evidence | Conclusion |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Observed versus fitted counts | In Q1, the observed zero proportion is `r extended_fitted_count_calibration$observed_zero_proportion[extended_fitted_count_calibration$fitted_count_quartile == "Q1: smallest fitted counts"]`, while the average fitted probability of zero satellites is `r extended_fitted_count_calibration$mean_fitted_zero_probability[extended_fitted_count_calibration$fitted_count_quartile == "Q1: smallest fitted counts"]`. In Q4, the observed zero proportion is `r extended_fitted_count_calibration$observed_zero_proportion[extended_fitted_count_calibration$fitted_count_quartile == "Q4: largest fitted counts"]`, while the average fitted probability of zero satellites is `r extended_fitted_count_calibration$mean_fitted_zero_probability[extended_fitted_count_calibration$fitted_count_quartile == "Q4: largest fitted counts"]`. | The extended model captures the ordering in the fitted mean structure, but it underestimates zero counts across the fitted-count range. |
| Pearson overdispersion |  | The training counts remain much more variable than the Classical Poisson mean-variance structure allows. |
| Excess zero counts | The training data contains `r extended_observed_zero_count` observed zero satellite counts, while the fitted extended model expects only `r formatC(extended_expected_zero_count, format = "f", digits = 2)` zeros. The zero-count $p$-value is `r formatC(extended_zero_count_p_value, format = "e", digits = 2)`. | The extended model still expects far fewer zero satellite counts than observed in the training data. |
| Analysis of Deviance |... | The extended model does not increase the **likelihood** function by a significant amount relative to the width-only model, so it likely **overfits** the noise in the training data.  |
| Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) |The width-only model has an AIC of `r formatC(simple_negative_binomial_aic, format = "f", digits = 3)` and the extended model has an AIC of `r formatC(extended_negative_binomial_aic, format = "f", digits = 3)` | The width-only Negative Binomial model is likely to have a better predictive performance than the extended model.
: Summary of goodness-of-fit conclusions for the extended Poisson regression model. {#tbl-negative-binomial-extended-gof-summary .striped .hover}

Overall, the width-only Negative Binomial regression model is correctly specified for the crabs data. The analysis of deviance test provides statistical evidence that the additional regressors do not significantly increase the **Negative Binomial likelihood** in comparison to the simple model; therefore, the width-only model is adequate to infer the relationship between satellite male counts and female crab characteristics. Moreover the smaller AIC score of the width-only model suggests that it is less likely to overfit in the context of **predictive performance**.


Let's continue with the simple Negative Binomial in our data science workflow, and use it to answer our **inferential** and **predictive inquiries** from [Section 11.3](http://localhost:54321/book/11-negative-binomial.html#sec-negative-binomial-study-design). There is some concern with zero counts in the train set, for which one can consider Zero-Inflated Poisson regression (@sec-zero-inflated-poisson) as an alternative.

### Interpreting Continuous Regressors {#sec-negative-binomial-continuous-regressors}

Because one kilogram is a large change for female crabs in this dataset, we should be careful not to compare the magnitude of the width and weight coefficients without considering their measurement units and the overlap between body-size measurements.
